title: Arrays, shapes, copies and views
outcome: Trace array storage and indexing while choosing deliberately between copies and shared views.
key_terms: The tuple of dimension lengths returned by `size`, which determines how indices map to elements.
Julia stores a matrix column by column, so looping over the first index in the innermost loop visits memory contiguously.
An array created with `view` or `@views` that refers to its parent's memory, so writing through it changes the parent.
The `copy` function duplicates the outer container but shares inner mutable elements, while `deepcopy` duplicates them as well.
Two names or arrays that refer to overlapping storage, so a write through one is visible through the other.
approach: Separate shape from contents and storage from interpretation. `size` reports axes, column-major order explains where `reshape(1:6, 2, 3)` puts each value, ordinary slicing copies, `view` shares storage, `copy` is shallow and `deepcopy` duplicates nested arrays. Bounds checks stay on so a bad index fails visibly.

exercises.title: Read a shape
exercises.task: Compare a length 2 vector with a 2-by-1 matrix.
exercises.hint: Element count does not determine the number of axes.
exercises.answer: Operations can dispatch or broadcast differently for these shapes.
exercises.why: `zeros(2)` has one axis with size `(2,)`, while `zeros(2, 1)` has two axes with size `(2, 1)`, even though both hold two numbers.
exercises.wrong: Treating both as the same column of two values can make matrix multiplication or broadcasting produce a different shape than intended.

exercises.title: Trace column order
exercises.task: Locate value 5 in the reshaped matrix.
exercises.hint: Follow columns through the input vector.
exercises.answer: The storage order is explicit and should not be confused with the scientific interpretation of axes.
exercises.why: Column-major filling puts 1 and 2 in column 1, 3 and 4 in column 2, and 5 and 6 in column 3, so 5 sits at row 1, column 3.
exercises.wrong: Reading the vector row by row places 5 at row 2, column 2, which is the row-major layout used by NumPy defaults.

exercises.title: Take a snapshot
exercises.task: Mutate an ordinary slice from a vector.
exercises.expected: The original scalar-element vector is unchanged.
exercises.answer: A snapshot protects later reads from this mutation, with an allocation cost.
exercises.why: `v[1:2]` allocates a new vector, so setting its first element changes only the copy and `v` keeps its values.
exercises.wrong: Expecting slices to share memory, as NumPy basic slices do, predicts that the original changes when it does not.
exercises.verify: Mutate the slice and assert the original still equals its starting contents.

exercises.title: Use a shared window
exercises.task: Mutate a view of the same range.
exercises.hint: A view refers to existing storage.
exercises.answer: A view is useful when shared mutation or avoided copying is intended.
exercises.why: `view(v, 1:2)` refers to the same storage, so writing to the view writes into `v`.
exercises.wrong: Using `@view` as a speed trick and then mutating the result silently alters data that other code still reads.
exercises.verify: Write 99 through the view and assert `v[1] == 99`.

exercises.title: Copy nested state
exercises.task: Compare copy and deepcopy on a vector of vectors.
exercises.expected: A shallow copy shares inner vectors; a deep copy does not in this fixture.
exercises.hint: Inspect both outer and inner identities.
exercises.answer: The required independence level depends on the data structure and algorithm.
exercises.why: `copy(nested)` makes a new outer vector holding the same inner vectors, so `shallow[1][1] = 9` changes `nested[1][1]` as well.
exercises.wrong: Assuming `copy` is enough for independence leaves inner arrays shared, so updates leak back into the original.
exercises.verify: The reference checks `nested[1][1] == 9` after the shallow edit and that it stays 9 after editing the `deepcopy`.

exercises.title: Retain a bound check
exercises.task: Read index 0 from a standard two-element vector.
exercises.hint: The valid standard indices start at 1.
exercises.answer: Bounds checking makes a violated indexing contract observable before considering lower-level optimizations.
exercises.why: Standard vectors start at index 1, so `[1, 2][0]` is outside `1:2` and raises `BoundsError`.
exercises.wrong: Disabling bounds checking with `@inbounds` before the indices are proven valid turns this clear error into reading arbitrary memory.
exercises.verify: Assert `@test_throws BoundsError [1, 2][0]` as the reference does.

checks_note: Shape checks show that `zeros(2, 1)` is a two by one matrix while `zeros(2)` is a vector of size `(2,)`, two different types despite holding the same count. Indexing at 0 throws because arrays start at 1. The nested copy lines prove that `copy` duplicates only the outer vector: writing 9 through `shallow` reaches `nested`, while the later write through `deepcopy` leaves `nested[1][1]` at 9.
